source_text:
ἀφελῶ τὸν φραγμὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ
ἔσται εἰς διαρπαγήν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τὴν 309 ἀσφάλειαν τοῦ πνεύματος. τί δὲ τὸ
μεσότοιχον; τὸ πρὸς τοὺς Ἕλληνας ἄμικτον· κεκώλυτο γὰρ Ἕλλησιν ἐπιμίγνυσθαι
Ἰουδαίους, ἵναμὴ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι εἰς τὴν εἰδωλολατρείαν καταπέσωσιν, οἱ καὶ χωρὶς
τούτου εἰδωλολατροῦντες. καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν ὃ λέγει ∆αυίδ· ὁ θεὸς κατοικίζει
μονοτρόπους ἐν οἴκῳ. ἔδει γὰρ τὸ προζύμιον ἰσχυρὸν γενέσθαι, ἵν' οὕτως τὸ ὅλον
τοῦ κόσμου ζυμωθῇ. Τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν τὸν νενομισμένον λέγει, ὡς ἀπὸ τῶν
ἐντολῶν τῶν Μωϋσαϊκῶν. ἐν δόγμασι, τοῖς ἰδίοις, καταργήσας, ὧν ἐστιν· οὐ τὰ
εἰσπορευόμενα κοινοῖ τὸν ἄνθρωπον–τοῦτο δὲ ἔλυεν τὸ τόδε φάγε, τόδε μὴ φάγῃς–,
καὶ τὸ μὴ διδόναι βιβλίον ἀποστασίου–τοῦτο ὑπεναντίως εἶχε πρὸς τὸ κατὰ πᾶσαν
αἰτίαν ἀφιέναι γυναῖκα–, καὶ τὸ ἡμέρας παρατηρεῖσθε καὶ μῆνας καὶ καιροὺς καὶ
ἐνιαυτούς– ἐναντίον ἦν οἷς ἔδωκε Μωϋσῆς. καὶ ὅλως πολλὰ τοιαῦτα ἐστὶ δογματικὰ
οἷς τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν κατήργησεν, οὐ τὰς ἐντολὰς ὡς ἀτόπους, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔθος
ὡς οὐκέτι χρησιμεῦον. αἱ γὰρ ἐντολαὶ τιμῶνται κἂν μὴ ἐνεργῶσιν, ὁ δὲ νόμος
λοιπόν, τοῦτ' ἔστι τὸ ὑπὸ νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς εἶναι ἔβλαπτε μετὰ τὴν
χάριν. Eph 2,15β–17 Ἕλληνες μὲν γὰρ τῆς εἰδωλολατρείας ὡς ἀσεβείας, Ἰουδαῖοι δὲ
τοῦ νόμου ὡς οὐκέτι χρησιμεύοντος ἀφιστάμενοι, εἰς ἑτέραν τινὰ καινότητα
εὐσεβείας ἀνοικοδομοῦνται. Ποιῶν εἰρήνην. ὁ γὰρ νόμος οὐ βούλεται εἰρήνην εἶναι.
διὰ τί; ἵνα μὴ ἡ εἰρήνη ἡ σωματικὴ πόλεμον κατὰ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἐγείρῃ. Ἀμφοτέρους
καταλλάξει τῷ θεῷ. ἐπειδὴ οἱ μὲν Ἕλληνες ἐπλανῶντο, οἱ δὲ Ἰουδαῖοι
παραβεβήκεσαν. Ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν αὐτῷ. πλάτος ἔχει τὸ νόημα ἐν συντομίᾳ
ῥήματος· ἐπειδὴ γὰρ νόμος ἦν ὁ διιστῶν Ἰουδαίους Ἑλλήνων κατὰ τὸ προειρημένον,
ἔμελλε δὲ παύεσθαι ὁ νόμος, οὐχ ἑτέρως δὲ ἐπαύσατο ἢ ἐπειδὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνέστη ὁ
κύριος ᾧ ἔδει συναφθῆναι τὴν ἐκκλησίαν ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μετὰ νόμον, λέγει ὅτι ἐν τῇ
σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ ἐκείνην τὴν ἔχθραν ἀπέκτεινε παύσας τὸν νόμον. 310 Καὶ ἐλθὼν
εὐηγγελίσατο εἰρήνην ὑμῖν τοῖς μακρὰν καὶ τοῖς ἐγγύς. τοῦτο δείκνυσιν ὅτι οὐκ
ἀσεβῆ τὸν νόμον λέγει τὸν Μωϋσέως ὡς τὸ εἰδωλολατρεῖν· μακρὰν γάρ φησιν εἶναι
τοὺς εἰδωλολάτρας, ἐγγὺς δὲ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους. τὸ δὲ ἐγγὺς καὶ μέρος εὐσεβείας
δείκνυσι καὶ οὐ τέλειον· εἰ γὰρ εἶχον τὸ τέλειον, οὐκ ἦσαν ἐγγύς, ἀλλ' ἐν αὐτῷ. εἰ δὲ
πάλιν ἦσαν ἐναντίοι, οὐκ ἦσαν ἐγγύς, ἀλλὰ πόρρωθεν μετὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων. Eph 3,2–3
Ἐνταῦθα βούλεται δεῖξαι, ὅτι οὐκ ἐπέρριψεν ὡς ἀλλοτρίοις καὶ ὑπ' ἄλλων
δεδιδαγμένοις, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐθνῶν κῆρυξ αἱρεθεὶς ἐχρεώστει καὶ τούτοις τὸ δεῖγμα, καὶ
ὅτι ὡς ὁ κύριος ἐδίδαξε τοὺς περὶ Ἰωάννην, οὕτω κἀμὲ κατ' ἀποκάλυψιν. ᾐνίξατο δὲ
ὅτι ἠδύνατο μὲν βαθύτερόν τι εἰπεῖν, συνεμετρήσατο δὲ τὴν διδασκαλίαν πρὸς ὅπερ
ἐχώρουν. Eph 3,10 Ἵνα γνωρισθῇ νῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς. εἰκότως· εἰ γὰρ ἐν τῷ θεῷ
ἐκέκρυπτο, ἠγνόουν πᾶσαι αἱ ἐξουσίαι. τὸν γὰρ νῦν οὐ τὸν τῆς χάριτος καιρὸν λέγει,
ἀλλ' ἀφ' οὗ προφῆται ἤρξαντο ἀποκαλύπτειν τὰ ἐσόμενα. Eph 3,15 Ἐν οὐρανοῖς,
φησίν, ἡ τῶν δικαίων διαγωγή, ἐπὶ γῆς δὲ ἡ πάντων ἀνθρώπων· οὐ γάρ εἰσι
τεταγμένοι ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς οἱ δίκαιοι μετὰ τῶν ζώντων, ἀλλ' ἰδιάζει ὥσπερ γενεά τις
ἐξαίρετος ἡ τῶν ἀνακειμένων τῷ θεῷ. καὶ λέγεται ἐπουράνιος μὲν ἡ γενεὰ τούτων
ὡς καθαρά, ἡ δὲ τῶν λοιπῶν γηΐνη ὥσπερ ἐρρυπωμένη.
thought_title: The law's dividing wall and its temporary customs
orientation: Severian is explaining Ephesians 2:14–17, arguing that Christ abolished the law's dividing customs between Jews and Greeks, not the commandments themselves.
pass_a_gloss: I will take away its fence and it will be for plundering, that is, the security of the Spirit. What then is the dividing wall? The non-mixing with the Greeks; for it had been forbidden for Jews to mix with Greeks, so that the Jews might not fall into idolatry, who even apart from this were committing idolatry. And this is what David says: God settles the solitary in a house. For it was necessary that the leaven become strong, so that thus the whole of the world might be leavened. He calls the law of commandments the one that had been customary, as from the commandments of Moses. In dogmas, his own, having abolished, of which it is: not the things entering in defile the man—but this was dissolving the 'eat this, do not eat that'—, and the not giving a bill of divorce—this was contrary to the dismissing a wife for every cause—, and the 'you observe days and months and seasons and years'—it was contrary to what Moses gave. And in general many such dogmatic things there are by which he abolished the law of commandments, not the commandments as inappropriate, but the custom as no longer useful. For the commandments are honored even if they are not in force, but the law henceforth, that is, the being under the law of commandments in our case, was harming after grace. Eph 2:15b–17 For Greeks, departing from idolatry as impiety, and Jews, departing from the law as no longer useful, are built up into some other newness of piety. Making peace. For the law does not wish peace to exist. Why? So that bodily peace may not stir up war against piety. He will reconcile both to God. Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed. Having killed the enmity in himself. The thought has breadth in brevity of expression; for since the law was what separated Jews from Greeks according to what was said before, and the law was about to cease, and it ceased in no other way than since the Lord rose from the dead, to whom the church had to be joined as to another husband after the law, he says that in his flesh he killed that enmity, having caused the law to cease. 310 And coming he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near. This shows that he does not call the law of Moses impious like idolatry; for he says the idolaters are far off, but the Jews near. And the 'near' shows a part of piety and not the perfect; for if they had the perfect, they would not be near, but in it. And if again they were opposed, they would not be near, but far off with the Greeks. Eph 3:2–3 Here he wishes to show that he did not cast it upon them as upon strangers and people taught by others, but that, having been chosen as herald of the nations, he owed also to these the demonstration, and that as the Lord taught those around John, so also me according to revelation. And he hinted that he could have said something deeper, but he measured the teaching to what they could contain. Eph 3:10 So that it might be made known now to the rulers. Reasonably; for if it had been hidden in God, all the powers were ignorant. For he calls 'now' not the time of grace, but from when the prophets began to reveal the things to come. Eph 3:15 In the heavens, he says, is the way of life of the righteous, and on earth that of all humans; for the righteous are not ranked on the earth with the living, but the generation of those dedicated to God stands apart like some special generation. And the generation of these is called heavenly as pure, but that of the rest earthly as defiled.

choices.english: I will take away its fence
choices.why: The future indicative is a prophetic citation; 'fence' (φραγμός) is distinct from the 'dividing wall' (μεσότοιχον) that Severian is explaining, so the distinction must be preserved.
Severian equates the fence with the Spirit's protection; 'security' captures ἀσφάλεια as protective safety, not mere certainty.
ἄμικτον is a neuter substantive adjective; 'non-mixing' preserves the abstract quality of the prohibition rather than turning it into a wall or barrier.

choices.term: τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν τὸν νενομισμένον
choices.english: the law of commandments that had been customary
choices.why: Severian distinguishes the commandments themselves from the temporary custom (ἔθος) of observing them; 'customary' renders νενομισμένον as established by custom, not by divine necessity.
rejected: the law of commandments as enacted
the law of commandments that was in force

choices.english: in dogmas, his own, having abolished
choices.why: The word order is deliberately awkward in Greek; 'his own' modifies 'dogmas' and refers to Christ's own teachings that replaced the old customs. Keeping the awkwardness preserves the emphasis.
rejected: having abolished in his own dogmas

choices.term: πλάτος ἔχει τὸ νόημα ἐν συντομίᾳ ῥήματος
choices.english: The thought has breadth in brevity of expression
choices.why: This is Severian's rhetorical comment on Paul's compressed phrasing; 'breadth' and 'brevity' form the contrast he intends.
rejected: the meaning is broad in a short phrase
the thought is wide in a brief word

pass_b_english: “I will take away its fence, and it will be plundered” (Isaiah 5:5). The fence means the security of the Spirit. What then is the dividing wall? It is the separation between Jews and Greeks. For Jews were forbidden to mix with Greeks, so that the Jews might not fall into idolatry, though even apart from this they were idolaters. And this is what David says: “God settles the solitary in a house” (Psalm 68:6). For the leaven had to become strong, so that in this way the whole world might be leavened.

Paul calls “the law of commandments” the law that had been established by custom, as from the commandments of Moses. He abolished it “in dogmas,” his own teachings. Among these are: “It is not what enters a person that defiles them” (Matthew 15:11). This dissolved the rule “eat this, do not eat that.” And the rule about giving a certificate of divorce: this stood in opposition to dismissing a wife for any cause. And “you observe days and months and seasons and years” (Galatians 4:10): this was contrary to what Moses had given. And in general there are many such dogmatic teachings by which he abolished the law of commandments, not the commandments as inappropriate, but the custom as no longer useful. For the commandments are honored even when they are not in force, but the law from then on, that is, our being under the law of commandments, was harmful after grace.

On Ephesians 2:15b–17: For Greeks, turning away from idolatry as impiety, and Jews, turning away from the law as no longer useful, are built up into a certain new way of piety. “Making peace.” For the law does not wish there to be peace. Why? So that bodily peace might not stir up war against piety. “He will reconcile both to God.” Since the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed.

“Having killed the hostility in himself.” The thought has breadth in brevity of expression. For since the law was what separated Jews from Greeks, as was said before, and the law was about to cease, and it ceased in no other way than because the Lord rose from the dead, to whom the church had to be joined as to another husband after the law, he says that in his flesh he killed that hostility by putting an end to the law.

“And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.” This shows that he does not call the law impious in the way idolatry is. For he says that the idolaters are far off, and the Jews near. But “near” indicates a partial piety, not a complete one. For if they had the complete, they would not be near but in it. And if, again, they were opposed, they would not be near but far off with the Greeks.

On Ephesians 3:2–3: Here Paul wants to show that he did not cast his message upon them as if they were strangers taught by others, but that, having been chosen as herald of the Gentiles, he owed them this demonstration too, and that just as the Lord taught those around John, so also he taught me by revelation. He hinted that he could have said something deeper, but he measured his teaching to what they could receive.

On Ephesians 3:10: “So that it might now be made known to the rulers.” Reasonably so. For if it had been hidden in God, all the authorities were ignorant of it. By “now” he does not mean the time of grace, but the time from which the prophets began to reveal the things to come.

On Ephesians 3:15: “In heaven,” he says, is the way of life of the righteous, and on earth that of all humanity. For the righteous are not ranked on earth with the living, but the generation of those devoted to God stands apart like some chosen race. And their generation is called heavenly as pure, while that of the rest is earthly as defiled.

problems.why: lint glossary: banned rendering of νόμος; use 'law' ('law of Moses')

fixed: The English already says 'the law of Moses' only in the phrase 'the law of Moses impious'; the source has νόμον τὸν Μωϋσέως, but the glossary bans 'Law of Moses' as a rendering of νόμος. The English is not using 'Law of Moses' as a title but as a descriptive phrase; however, to comply with the glossary, I changed it to 'the law impious'.

problems.quote: the rule not to give a certificate of divorce
problems.why: Source says 'the not giving a certificate of divorce'—Moses' command TO give divorce certificate (Deut 24:1). English 'rule not to give' inverts meaning; Christ abolished Moses' divorce permission, not a prohibition.
problems.fix: the rule about giving a certificate of divorce
problems.ruling: τὸ μὴ διδόναι = 'not giving'; source says Christ abolished Moses' rule of giving divorce certificates, not a prohibition.

edits.old: the rule not to give a certificate of divorce
edits.new: the rule about giving a certificate of divorce

fixed: The reported problem about 'the law of Moses impious' is not a real problem: the English 'he does not call the law impious in the way idolatry is' already says the same thing as the source, and the previous attempted edit was unnecessary.

last_rejected.quote: the leaven had to become strong
last_rejected.source_quote: ἔδει γὰρ τὸ προζύμιον ἰσχυρὸν γενέσθαι
last_rejected.why: 'prozymion' is starter-dough/leaven, but context suggests Jewish people as starter; 'leaven' alone misses typology.
last_rejected.fix: the starter-dough had to become strong
last_rejected.ruling: 'Leaven' correctly renders προζύμιον; 'become strong' captures ἰσχυρὸν γενέσθαι. Typological nuance is implicit, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: he says that in his flesh he killed that hostility
last_rejected.source_quote: λέγει ὅτι ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ ἐκείνην τὴν ἔχθραν ἀπέκτεινε
last_rejected.why: Ambiguous 'he': Paul (quoting) or Christ? Source has Paul speaking, English could clarify Paul says Christ...
last_rejected.fix: Paul says that in his flesh Christ killed that hostility
last_rejected.ruling: 'He says' renders λέγει; context (ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ αὐτοῦ) makes Christ the subject. Pronoun ambiguity is normal English, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: he owed them this demonstration too
last_rejected.why: 'deigma' means example/pattern, not demonstration; and 'too' is vague.
last_rejected.fix: he owed them this example as well
last_rejected.ruling: δεῖγμα can mean 'proof/demonstration'; 'owed' renders ἐχρεώστει. 'Too' translates καὶ τούτοις. Within normal range, not a major error.

polish.changed: Clarified the Isaiah quotation as Scripture, made the equation between the dividing wall and separation from Greeks explicit, smoothed ungrammatical phrasing about the law of commandments, rendered 'dogmas' as Christ's own teachings, changed 'newness of piety' to 'new way of piety,' and clarified speaker transitions and pronoun references throughout.

notes.why: Same concept of cosmic unity; 'brought together' and 'reconcile' may seem distinct to reader.
notes.fix: Use 'reconcile/unite' consistently or note equivalence.

notes.why: Same Greek ethos; 'custom' and 'customary' appear as noun and adjective but reader may not connect.
notes.fix: Use 'custom'/'customary' consistently with note.

notes.quote: the leaven had to become strong
notes.why: Metaphor unexplained; reader cannot connect to Jewish mission or parable of leaven.
notes.fix: Add note: leaven metaphor refers to Jewish faith spreading to world.

notes.why: Allusion to Hosea/remarriage imagery unexplained; reader cannot place this typology.
notes.fix: Note: alludes to Hosea and Pauline 'married to another' (Romans 7).

notes.quote: "I will take away its fence, and it will be plundered" (Isaiah 5:5)—that is, the security of the Spirit.
notes.why: Unclear whose words follow quote; 'that is' could be Severianus or catena interpolator.
notes.fix: Mark as Severianus's interpretation of Isaiah.

notes.why: Anachronistic or misleading; refers to Christ's teachings/decisions, not later 'dogmas' in ecclesiastical sense.
notes.fix: Use 'decrees' or 'teachings' with note.

notes.why: Unclear what this means; probably 'new way of piety' or 'renewed piety', awkward as rendered.
notes.fix: Revise to 'new manner of piety' or 'new form of devotion.'

variants.text: our being under the law of commandments

notes.why: Reader cannot tell if 'law,' 'commandments,' and 'law of commandments' are the same or different concepts.
notes.fix: Use one term consistently or define each at first use.

variants.text: Jews were forbidden to mix with Greeks

notes.why: 'Non-mixing' and 'dividing wall' refer to the same concept but use different wording without explicit equation.
notes.fix: State explicitly: 'The dividing wall is the non-mixing with the Greeks.'

notes.why: 'Dogmas' here means decrees or ordinances, not doctrines; untranslated Greek term may mislead.
notes.fix: Render as 'in decrees' or gloss as 'ordinances.'

notes.quote: I will take away its fence, and it will be plundered
notes.why: Isaiah 5:5 is quoted without attribution; reader may think Severianus is speaking.
notes.fix: Add '(Isaiah 5:5)' inline before the quote.

notes.quote: He calls "the law of commandments" the one that had been customary, as from the commandments of Moses.
notes.why: 'The one that had been customary' is ungrammatical; 'one' has no clear antecedent.
notes.fix: Rewrite: 'He calls the law of commandments the customary law derived from Moses' commandments.'

polish.changed: Clarified speakers and pronouns, smoothed transitions between sections, made the fence-to-Spirit connection explicit, and adjusted phrasing for natural modern reading while preserving all claims and quotations.

notes.quote: I multiplied visions and was likened through the prophets
notes.why: Hosea 12:10 cited without book name
notes.fix: Add '(Hosea 12:10)' attribution

notes.quote: God settles the solitary in a house
notes.why: Psalm 68:6 cited without context of David
notes.fix: Add 'as David says' or Psalm identifier

notes.why: Rhetorical question without clear speaker marker after Isaiah quote
notes.fix: Add 'Severianus asks:'

notes.quote: That is, the security of the Spirit. What then is the dividing wall?
notes.why: 'That is' refers to fence, but 'security of the Spirit' is unexplained leap
notes.fix: Explain Isaiah 5:5 refers to vineyard; 'fence' is law's protection

notes.why: Greek 'en dogmasin' usually 'by decrees' or 'in ordinances'; 'dogmas' sounds anachronistically doctrinal
notes.fix: Use 'decrees' or 'teachings' consistently

variants.text: Jews were forbidden to mix with Greeks
For Greeks, turning away from idolatry

notes.why: 'Greeks' is used for Gentiles/non-Jews; modern readers may think ethnic Greeks specifically.
notes.fix: Use 'Gentiles' or 'non-Jews' consistently, noting 'Greeks' = Gentiles.

notes.why: Reader may not understand this refers to Mosaic ceremonial law, not moral law.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'law of commandments' = the Mosaic ceremonial regulations.

notes.quote: He abolished it "in dogmas," his own teachings.
notes.why: 'In dogmas' is ambiguous; reader may think Christ abolished the law by his own dogmas.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'in dogmas' means 'in decrees/regulations,' referring to the law's ordinances.

notes.quote: On Ephesians 2:15b–17: For Greeks, turning away from idolatry as impiety
notes.why: Reader cannot tell if these are Severianus's words or a quoted opponent's position.
notes.fix: Mark clearly as Severianus's own commentary on the cited verses.

notes.quote: On Ephesians 3:2–3: Here he wants to show
notes.why: Transition between sections is abrupt; 'he' = Paul is assumed but not stated.
notes.fix: Clarify that 'he' refers to Paul throughout these comments.

notes.quote: For the leaven had to become strong, so that in this way the whole world might be leavened.
notes.why: The leaven metaphor is introduced without explanation; reader may not connect it to the church's growth.
notes.fix: Note: leaven = the church/faith, which must be concentrated first to spread through the world.
